text: The latest update did not improve battery life at all.
rationale: This example uses negation before the positive cue improve to test whether the model catches the negative meaning.

text: This app is not bad after the update.
rationale: This example uses negation before bad to test whether the model understands that not bad is mildly positive.

text: The app does not crash now.
rationale: This example includes the negative trigger crash but negates it, making the intended sentiment positive.

text: I cannot say this app is terrible anymore.
rationale: This example negates a strong negative word to test whether the model relies on terrible or understands the full sentence.

text: It is not useful for my work.
rationale: This example negates the positive word useful to test whether the model catches the negative meaning.

text: This app is no longer reliable on my phone.
rationale: This example contains the positive cue reliable but the phrase no longer flips the sentiment to negative.

text: Great idea, poor execution.
rationale: This example starts with the positive cue great but ends with a negative judgment.

text: The design is beautiful but the app is unusable.
rationale: This example tests whether the model overweights beautiful and misses unusable.

text: Fast download, but every file becomes corrupted.
rationale: This example includes the positive cue fast but the actual user experience is negative.

text: The update is impressive only because it broke fewer things than last time.
rationale: This example uses a positive cue impressive while describing a negative comparison.

text: The company reported a 20 percent increase in quarterly revenue.
rationale: This business-news sentence is factual reporting, not a consumer app opinion.

text: The actor announced a new film during the festival press event.
rationale: This entertainment-news sentence has no clear app-review sentiment.

text: The cybersecurity team investigated an attack on the network.
rationale: This news sentence contains the negative word attack but reports an event rather than user sentiment.

text: The recipe calls for fresh basil and a slow simmer.
rationale: This non-app domain sentence tests whether the classifier forces sentiment onto unrelated prose.

text: The team won the final match after a late goal.
rationale: This sports sentence may sound positive but is factual reporting rather than app sentiment.

text: Works.
rationale: This very short review tests whether the model can classify minimal positive text.

text: Broken again.
rationale: This very short review tests whether the model can classify minimal negative text.

text: Okay.
rationale: This very short review tests whether the model can handle ambiguous minimal neutral text.

text: After the update I opened the app, tried to log in, waited for the loading screen, restarted my phone, cleared the cache, reinstalled everything, and still could not access my account, so I finally gave up.
rationale: This long sentence tests whether the model preserves the negative meaning across many details.

text: I like the clean layout, the fast loading time, the simple menus, and the helpful notifications, although I still think the search feature could be improved in a future update.
rationale: This long sentence tests whether the model handles mixed but mostly positive feedback.

text: Great, another update that broke everything.
rationale: This sarcastic sentence uses the positive word great to express negative sentiment.

text: Amazing work making the app slower than before.
rationale: This sarcastic sentence uses amazing positively on the surface but the intended meaning is negative.

text: Perfect, now I have to restart the app every five minutes.
rationale: This sarcastic sentence uses perfect while describing a negative failure.

text: Love waiting forever for a page to load.
rationale: This sarcastic sentence uses love but describes a frustrating experience.

text: Fantastic job removing the only feature I used.
rationale: This sarcastic sentence uses fantastic but the user is complaining.

text: The app is fine, but I would not recommend it.
rationale: This example tests mixed sentiment where fine may look neutral but the recommendation is negative.

text: I do not love it, but it gets the job done.
rationale: This example tests mild mixed sentiment where the user is neither clearly positive nor negative.

text: The app is simple, stable, and boring in the best way.
rationale: This example tests whether boring is treated as negative even when the phrase says it is positive.

text: Nothing changed after the update.
rationale: This example tests whether lack of change is treated as neutral rather than negative.

text: It works for basic tasks, but power users will be disappointed.
rationale: This example tests mixed audience-specific sentiment where the overall label is neutral.
